newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Shooting, delays place questions over Albania vote.
newsitem.headline: Shooting, delays place questions over Albania vote.

text.p: Question marks dogged Albania's election after shooting at a rally sent Tirana residents scurrying for cover and delays in counting votes prompted the West to warn authorities to cooperate or face an aid cut-off.

Although the Socialists are coasting to victory after last Sunday's first round, counting was still incomplete late on Thursday, with two days remaining before run-off ballots in at least 25 districts.
That posed big big logistical headaches for the Organisation for Security and Cooperation (OSCE), responsible for overseeing the vote and printing ballot papers.

Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen, current OSCE chairman, urged President Sali Berisha and political parties "to cease forthwith any attempt to put obstacles in the way of the electoral process."

He said future foreign aid to Albania, Europe's poorest country shattered by months of violence and 1,500 deaths, "will depend on the willingness of the Albanian authorities to cooperate on democratic reform".
Berisha, who has pledged to resign once a leftist government is in place, told Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi the election would be completed smoothly.

A statement issued by Prodi's office in Rome said Italian authorities "were given assurances of the will on the part of the government and of local political forces to carry out the electoral process to the end in the best conditions".

Election officials said counting was finished in all but seven of 115 districts by Thursday evening but gave no detailed breakdown. Earlier results had given the Socialists and their allies 49 seats to eight for Berisha's Democratic Party.
Security problems in the country were compounded by the resignation on Thursday of Interior Minister Belul Celo.

He quit amid a struggle for control of Albania's security forces between Berisha, who also has pledged to step down in view of the defeat of his Democratic Party, and Socialist Prime Minister Bashkim Fino.
Thursday's shooting erupted at a march by royalists who accuse the victorious Socialists of rigging a referendum, also held last Sunday, in which voters rejected restoration of the monarchy.

Albanian officials said one person was killed outside Central Election Commission offices, where counting was in progress. Partial returns show a 64 to 36 percent margin against putting self-proclaimed king Leka on the throne.
The firing started as Leka, dressed in battle fatigues and grey beret and sporting two pistols of his own, neared the building after marching from central Skanderbeg Square.
Hundreds of people scattered behind buildings and cars. The volleys, apparently mostly in the air, went on for 10 minutes.
Monarchists said police started the shooting and blamed the government but police denied they had fired first. Officials inside the building said the first shots came from protesters.
The incident plunged the city into confusion and quickly turned into a political football.

Berisha's Democrats said "snipers" had carried out the shooting and blamed the Socialists for spreading false information about the outcome of the referendum. Socialist Prime Minister Fino suggested the monarchists were being manipulated, but said nothing about who might be responsible.
Leka's backers vowed to gather again on Friday evening.

"You are starting a war which can only ignite a big conflagration," Leka's 'court minister' Abedin Mulsmanaj said in a statement addressed to Fino's government. "You are shooting at people staging peaceful protests."

Leka, who returned to Albania in April after spending nearly his entire life in exile, had little effect on the hard-fought general election campaign, drawing only small crowds at rallies. His father was King Zog, a tribal chieftain who became Albania's president and proclaimed himself king in 1928.
